The question: "Two residues in this structure are closer together than their atomic radii allow, producing the single most severe steric clash in the structure. Compare heavy atoms in different residues using overlap = r1 + r2 - 0.40 - distance, in Angstrom, with Bondi van der Waals radii. Exclude atom pairs connected by one or two covalent bonds, pairs involving a metal ion, and every sulfur SG-SG atom pair, regardless of its distance or whether it is identified as a disulfide bond. Rank residue pairs by their largest remaining positive atom-pair overlap. Which residue pair is it? Answer with a residue pair joined by a double hyphen."

We need to find the pair of residues that have the largest positive overlap (i.e., severe steric clash) among heavy atoms (non-hydrogen atoms) in different residues, excluding certain pairs.

Then compare overlaps across all residue pairs, exclude pairs that are covalently connected (one or two bonds) or involve metal ion (ZN). Also exclude any SG-SG atom pair (i.e., cysteine SG atoms) regardless of distance. Then find the pair with the largest positive overlap.

We need to compute heavy atoms for each residue: N, CA, C, O, CB, CG, etc. For each residue type, we need Bondi radii for each atom. The typical Bondi vdW radii: H:1.2, C:1.70, N:1.55, O:1.52, S:1.80, P:1.80, etc. But the question says "Compare heavy atoms in different residues using overlap = r1 + r2 - 0.40 - distance, in Angstrom, with Bondi van der Waals radii." So we need to use Bondi radii for each heavy atom. Usually the radii: C: 1.70, N: 1.55, O: 1.52, S: 1.80, P: 1.80, Cl: 1.75, etc. But we need to be careful: The formula includes -0.40. That is typical for "overlap" calculation: Overlap = (r1 + r2) - (distance + 0.4). Actually typical formula for steric clash: overlap = (r1 + r2) - (distance + 0.4). So here they define overlap = r1 + r2 - 0.40 - distance. So if distance is less than r1 + r2 - 0.40, overlap > 0.

Thus we need to compute overlaps for all pairs of heavy atoms from different residues that are not covalently connected (covalent bonds within same residue are excluded; also pairs that are one or two covalent bonds apart (i.e., in adjacent residues that are linked by a peptide bond? Actually covalent bonds within a residue are the side chain bonds; also the peptide backbone N-C and C-N bonds are within the same residue (N of residue to CA of next? Actually the backbone N of residue i is covalently bonded to C of residue i-1? Wait the peptide bond connects C of residue i-1 to N of residue i. So the N of residue i is covalently bonded to C of residue i-1, which is also part of the same chain. So any pair of atoms that are within the same residue (including side chain atoms) are excluded because they are covalently connected (one bond or two bonds? Actually within a residue, the backbone atoms are connected by covalent bonds: N-CA, CA-C, C-O, etc. Also side chain atoms have covalent bonds to CB, etc. So any pair within the same residue is excluded. Also pairs that are one or two covalent bonds apart across residues? For example, the CB of residue i and the CA of residue i+1 are not covalently bonded (they are separated by a peptide bond). However, the bond between CA of residue i and C of residue i is covalent; the N of residue i+1 is covalently bonded to the C of residue i. So the N of residue i+1 is one bond away from the C of residue i (the peptide bond). So we need to exclude pairs that are one or two covalent bonds apart. That includes the N of residue i+1 and the C of residue i (the peptide bond). Also the CA of residue i and the N of residue i+1 are separated by two bonds? Actually CA of residue i is bonded to N of residue i (within same residue). Then N of residue i is covalently bonded to C of residue i-1, but not directly to CA of residue i+1. The N of residue i+1 is bonded to C of residue i. So the N of residue i+1 is one bond away from C of residue i, which is two bonds away from CA of residue i (CA of i to C of i is one bond, C of i is bonded to N of i+1 is second bond). So the pair of CA of i and N of i+1 is two bonds apart. So we need to exclude those pairs as well.

Thus we need to compute overlaps for all heavy atom pairs that are not within same residue, not covalently connected (i.e., not directly bonded or within two bonds). Also exclude pairs involving metal ion ZN. Also exclude any SG-SG atom pair (cysteine SG atoms) regardless of distance. So we need to identify all cysteine residues: A:128 (CYS), A:130 (CYS), A:135 (CYS), A:184 (CYS), A:256 (CYS), A:282 (CYS). Actually also A:?? Let's list: CYS A 128, CYS A 130, CYS A 135, CYS A 184, CYS A 256, CYS A 282. Also A:?? There's also A:?? Then A:256 is CYS. Then A:282 is CYS. So there are six cysteines.

We need to find the most severe clash, i.e., the pair with the largest positive overlap. That is the pair with the smallest distance relative to sum of radii.

We can try to identify candidate pairs by looking at the coordinates and seeing which residues are close. Let's compute distances between backbone atoms of consecutive residues (i and i+1) but exclude those covalently bonded. The backbone N of residue i+1 is covalently bonded to C of residue i (peptide bond). So exclude N(i+1) - C(i). The CA of residue i is covalently bonded to N(i) and C(i) (within same residue). So exclude CA(i) - N(i) and CA(i) - C(i). But CA(i) is covalently bonded to N(i) (within same residue) and C(i) (within same residue). So those pairs are excluded anyway because they are within same residue. The backbone N(i) is covalently bonded to C(i-1) (previous residue). So exclude N(i) - C(i-1). The backbone C(i) is covalently bonded to N(i+1) (next residue). So exclude C(i) - N(i+1). So the backbone atoms across residues that are covalently bonded are excluded. The other backbone atoms across residues: N(i+1) - C(i) (peptide bond) excluded. N(i+1) - CA(i) are two bonds apart (CA(i)-C(i)-N(i+1) is three bonds? Actually CA(i) is bonded to C(i) (1), C(i) is bonded to N(i+1) (2). So CA(i) to N(i+1) is two bonds apart. The question says exclude pairs connected by one or two covalent bonds. So CA(i) - N(i+1) is two bonds apart, so excluded. Similarly, N(i+1) - C(i) is one bond (the peptide bond). So excluded. So any backbone atoms across residues are likely excluded due to being within two bonds. Let's verify: N(i) is bonded to C(i-1) (one bond). So N(i) - C(i-1) excluded. N(i) - C(i) is within same residue, excluded. N(i) - CA(i) within same residue excluded. N(i) - N(i+1) not directly bonded, but are they within two bonds? N(i) - C(i) - N(i+1) is two bonds (C(i) is bonded to both N(i) and N(i+1)). So N(i) - N(i+1) is two bonds apart. So exclude. N(i) - CA(i+1) is three bonds? N(i) - C(i) - N(i+1) - CA(i+1) is three bonds. So N(i) - CA(i+1) is three bonds, not excluded. However, N(i) - CA(i+1) is across residues, but not covalently bonded. So we could consider that pair. However, it's less likely to be a severe clash because backbone atoms are not usually that close.
